o: We must read `words.txt`, split its contents into words (separated by one or more spaces), count occurrences of each word, and print each word with its count sorted by descending frequency. In the example, 'the' appears 4 times, 'is' 3, 'sunny' 2, and 'day' 1. Since the file contains only lowercase letters and spaces, no punctuation or case handling is needed — we only need robust whitespace splitting. The note about unique frequencies means a plain sort by count is sufficient; the one-line hint points to composing classic Unix text tools via pipes.
k: `tr -s ' '` squeezes repeated spaces so every word becomes one token per line after translating spaces to newlines.
`sort | uniq -c` is the canonical Unix idiom for counting duplicates.
`sort -rn` sorts numerically in reverse to produce descending frequency order.
The whole solution composes into a single pipeline of small, single-purpose tools.

a.n: Approach 1: Classic Unix Pipeline (tr / sort / uniq / sort)
a.i: Translate spaces into newlines so each word sits on its own line, squeeze repeats so blank lines vanish, then use `uniq -c` to count consecutive identical lines (after sorting). Finally sort numerically descending on the count column. This is the idiomatic one-line shell answer.
s: Use `tr -s ' ' '\n'` to convert runs of spaces into single newlines, putting each word on its own line.
Pipe through `sort` so equal words become adjacent.
Pipe through `sort -rn` to order by count descending and print.
a.t: O(n log n) where n is the number of words — dominated by the two sorts.
a.sp: O(n) to hold all words as lines during sorting.

a.i: awk splits each input line into fields on whitespace automatically, so counting is just incrementing an associative array keyed by the word. A final END block prints entries sorted by count using a shell sort call or gawk's asort. This avoids intermediate files entirely.
s: For each field of each line, increment counts[$1..$NF].
In the END block, print each word and count piped through `sort -k2 -rn`.
a.t: O(n log n) due to the final sort of distinct words.
a.sp: O(d) where d is the number of distinct words stored in the associative array.

w: For this shell problem, submit the one-liner: `cat words.txt | tr -s ' ' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | awk '{print $2, $1}'`. The trailing awk (or `sed`) reformats `uniq -c`'s '<count> <word>' output into '<word> <count>'. Common pitfalls: forgetting `-s` in tr (leaving empty lines that uniq would count), forgetting `-r`/`-n` in the final sort (wrong order or lexicographic sort of numbers like '10' < '9'), and outputting columns in the wrong order. Follow-ups may ask for top-k words (`head -k`), handling arbitrary whitespace including tabs (`tr -s '[:space:]' '\n'`), or streaming solutions without sorting all data (use awk hash counting plus a heap).
